Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Electra Motors Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question during this time, please press star then one on your telephone keypad. If you're using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Electra Motors' Q2 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Elena Vasquez, CEO; Raj Patel, CFO; Mike Thompson, Chief Manufacturing Officer; Dr. Lisa Chen, Chief Technology Officer; Carlos Mendoza, Chief Supply Chain Officer; Sarah Klein, Chief Sales Officer; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Elena Vasquez.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Reflecting on Q2, we are proud of the significant strides Electra Motors has made across all facets of our business. We have achieved remarkable progress in changes to our order backlog and reservation trends, reductions in battery costs per kWh, the positive impact of our pricing strategies and promotional activities, our capital expenditure plans and investment priorities, overall company performance highlights and key achievements, delivery volumes by model and geographic region, gross margins per vehicle, and delivery volume guidance by model. The market reception to our Electra Apex SUV has been overwhelmingly positive, with the associated surge in demand far exceeding our initial estimates.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Raj Patel to discuss our financial performance in greater detail.

Raj Patel:
Thank you, Elena. Good morning, everyone. Our revenue for Q2 reached $2.8 billion, marking an exceptional 45% increase compared to the same period last year. Our gross margin expanded to 24.5%, driven by enhanced operational efficiencies and a favorable product mix. Operating expenses amounted to $650 million, resulting in a net income of $320 million. Our financial position remains strong, with $4.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We anticipate revenue of $3.2 to $3.5 billion for the upcoming quarter.

Good afternoon, everyone—though it's morning here, thank you for joining our Q2 2024 earnings call. Before I dive into the P&L and balance sheet, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our order backlog and reservation trends, as these are leading indicators of our demand pipeline and production scalability in the hyper-competitive EV landscape. Our backlog represents firm customer orders not yet fulfilled, while reservations capture refundable interest in our upcoming models—a metric we've refined since our 2022 IPO to better reflect consumer intent amid volatile supply chains.

At the end of Q2, our global order backlog stood at $18.7 billion, up 22% year-over-year from $15.3 billion and 8% quarter-over-quarter from $17.3 billion in Q1. This equates to approximately 285,000 unfulfilled vehicles at our blended average selling price of $65,600—a slight uptick from $64,200 last quarter, driven by a higher mix of our premium Electra Apex SUV. Our reservation book—primarily for the forthcoming Electra Bolt compact crossover and the high-performance Apex GT variant—grew to 142,000 units, a robust 35% YoY increase from 105,000 units and 12% QoQ from 127,000. Conversion rates remain strong at 68% over the trailing 12 months, well above industry peers like Rivian around 55% and Lucid in the mid-40s, reflecting our disciplined refund policy and real-time delivery transparency via our app-based configurator.

Breaking it down by model, the star performer is our Electra Apex SUV, which accounts for 62% of backlog at $11.6 billion, or 176,000 units. Deliveries ramped 45% QoQ to 28,500 units, but demand outpaced supply due to gigacasting bottlenecks at our Texas GigaFactory—we've since certified our second 9,000-ton Giga Press, targeting 20% throughput gains by Q4. The workhorse Electra Prime sedan holds 28% at $5.2 billion, or 85,000 units, bolstered by fleet wins including a 12,000-unit order from Hertz for urban ride-share. Legacy ICE-to-EV conversions represent just 10% at $1.9 billion, down from 15% YoY as we sunset those lines.

Reservations skew heavily toward the Bolt, with 89,000 units or 63% of total, fueled by its sub-$40k MSRP qualifying for the full $7,500 IRA point-of-sale rebate. Early GT reservations hit 53,000, with 40% from performance enthusiasts—think Plaid-level 1,020 hp and 250-mile range on LFP cells, positioning us against Tesla's Cyberbeast and Lucid's Air Sapphire.

Regionally, North America dominates at 71% of backlog or $13.3 billion, up 28% YoY on IRA tailwinds and lease penetration hitting 42% versus 32% industry average per Cox Automotive. Europe contributes 18% at $3.4 billion, flat QoQ but up 15% YoY despite softer German demand amid subsidy phase-outs; our Berlin plant's 4680 cell integration has unlocked 15% range gains to 420 miles WLTP, winning EU fleet tenders. China/Asia-Pacific is 11% at $2.0 billion, down 5% QoQ due to BYD's Seagull price wars—we've countered with localized LFP packs via our CATL JV, pricing the Prime at RMB 220k to claw back share. Emerging markets like India added 8,000 reservations post our Q1 showroom launches.

What's driving these trends? First, supply chain resilience: Q2 inventory days on hand fell to 42 from 58 in Q1, thanks to our vertical integration—in-house 4680 production now covers 65% of cells, reducing reliance on Panasonic/LG. Second, technical initiatives: OTA software update 4.2 boosted Apex efficiency 8% via predictive thermal management, triggering 15,000 pull-forward orders. Third, incentives and mix: Full Self-Driving beta uptake at 52% drove $4,200 ASP uplift; our $99/mo. FSD subscription is converting 22% of reservation holders pre-delivery.

Strategically, these metrics validate our 'Ramp-to-Scale' playbook. We're on track for 350,000 annual run-rate by year-end at Texas and Berlin, with Arizona GigaFactory breaking ground Q4 for 500k capacity by 2026—funded via $2.5B convertible notes closed last month. Backlog visibility gives us 18 months of FCF-positive production at 25% gross margins, up from 21% Q1. Risks? Potential IRA clawbacks or China tariffs, but our 40% US content shields us. Looking ahead, we guide Q3 backlog growth to $20B+ and reservations to 160k, assuming 10% ASP stability.

This positions Electra Motors not just as a volume player like BYD or legacy OEMs, but a premium innovator like Tesla 2.0—with backlog-to-revenue conversion at 85% LTM.

Before we open the line for Q&A, I'd like to dive deep into one of the most critical levers driving our profitability and scalability: battery costs per kWh. Batteries represent roughly 35-40% of our total vehicle BOM—bill of materials—and getting this right is table stakes in the EV race. All data here is at the pack level, inclusive of cells, modules, BMS, and thermal management.

For Q2, our average battery pack cost landed at $98 per kWh, a robust 18% decline year-over-year from $119/kWh in Q2 2023. On a sequential basis, that's down 5% from $103/kWh in Q1. This puts us at the sharp end of the industry curve—Benchmark Mineral Intelligence pegged the global average at $132/kWh for 2023 packs, with cell-level averages around $109/kWh. For context, our fleet mix skews toward our mid-range Electra Prime sedan and the new Apex Max SUV, both leveraging 60-100 kWh packs, so this translates to $6,500-$9,000 per vehicle in battery spend, versus $11,000+ at prior rates.

What drove this? Three buckets: scale efficiencies, chemistry shifts, and manufacturing innovations. On scale, our Nevada Gigafactory Phase 2 ramped to 25 GWh annualized output in Q2, up 40% QoQ, unlocking 12-15% cost arbitrage through higher utilization and localized sourcing. Material costs helped too—lithium carbonate spot prices fell 65% YoY to around $12,000/tonne, per Fastmarkets, while nickel sulfate dipped 30%—directly flowing through to our NMC 811 cells, which comprise 70% of our mix.

Chemistry-wise, we've accelerated our pivot to LFP for entry-level packs, now at 25% of volume up from 10% last year. Sourced via our JV with CATL, these Shanghai Megafactory cells clock in at $72/kWh cell-level, enabling sub-$90/kWh packs in our Electra Bolt commuter. LFP's iron-phosphate stability gives us a 20% edge in thermal runaway margins over NMC, critical for our fast-charging roadmap targeting 400 kW DC.

Industry-wide, BloombergNEF projects pack costs hitting $80/kWh by 2027 and sub-$60/kWh by 2030, driven by a 15-20% CAGR decline—mirroring the 89% drop since 2010. But we're outpacing that: our internal models forecast $75/kWh average by end-2026, contingent on gigafactory full ramp and next-gen adoption. Key tailwinds include cell-to-pack architectures, which eliminate modules to shave 15-20% off assembly costs—we're at 65% CTP adoption today, targeting 90% by 2025, akin to Tesla's 4680 structural packs. Dry electrode coating, rolled out in our Q3 pilot line with Panasonic, cuts slurry costs by 30% and boosts energy density to 280 Wh/kg from 260 Wh/kg.

Regionally, China dominates low-cost LFP at $55-65/kWh cell-level—BYD's Blade batteries are sub-$50/kWh at scale—thanks to 70% global capacity share and domestic supply chains. Europe and the US lag at $120-140/kWh due to higher labor and ESG premiums, but the IRA's $35/kWh domestic content credit and EU Battery Regulation are game-changers. Our US content hit 65% in Q2 up from 45%, qualifying for full incentives on 80% of Nevada output, effectively netting $20-25/kWh subsidy value. South Korea's LGES and Samsung SDI are closing the gap with prismatic NCM cells under $90/kWh, but China's overcapacity—CATL alone at 390 GWh planned for 2025—could pressure pricing further, a risk we're hedging via multi-supplier contracts.

Strategically, vertical integration is core: 40% of our cells are now in-house via Electra Cellworks, with silicon-anode pilots yielding 15% density gains and 10% cost savings over graphite. We're investing $2.5B in solid-state R&D, partnering with QuantumScape for sulfide-based cells targeting $50/kWh and 600 Wh/kg by 2028—prototype validation in H2 2025. Recycling closes the loop: our Redwood Materials JV processed 5,000 tonnes of black mass in Q2, recovering 95% nickel and 92% lithium at $5-7/kWh credit, scaling to 50 GWh equivalent by 2027.

Risks? Supply chain volatility—cobalt up 10% on DRC unrest—and capex intensity, with $1.2B CapEx this year on batteries alone. But our gross margins expanded 450 bps YoY to 28.5%, with batteries contributing 60% of that. Looking ahead, we see sub-$100/kWh as the unlock for mass-market parity with ICE, and we're positioned to lead.

Today, I'd like to dive deep into the impact of our pricing strategies and promotional activities, which were pivotal in navigating a dynamic EV market characterized by softening demand signals, intensifying competition from Tesla's Model 3/Y price adjustments and BYD's aggressive exports, and macroeconomic headwinds like elevated interest rates. Our approach delivered a 12% quarter-over-quarter volume growth to 85,000 units globally, while protecting our core profitability metrics.

On average selling prices, we saw a modest 3% sequential decline in blended ASP to $48,200, primarily driven by a higher mix of our entry-level Electra Bolt Compact SUV, which accounted for 42% of deliveries—up from 35% last quarter. This model's base MSRP of $39,900 held firm, but realized ASP came in at $42,500 after incentives, reflecting our targeted promotions. Conversely, our premium Electra Prime Sedan ASP rose 5% to $62,800, bolstered by optional LFP battery upgrades and our new 800V architecture fast-charging suite, which added $4,200 in average attach rates. Overall, this mix shift compressed gross margins by 210 basis points to 22.4%, but we offset much of that through supply chain efficiencies, including a 15% reduction in 4680 cell costs via our Nevada Gigafactory ramp-up.

Promotional activities were our volume accelerator amid a 2% YoY decline in U.S. EV registrations per Cox Automotive data. We deployed a multi-tiered incentive stack totaling $1.8 billion globally—up 25% from Q1—focusing on lease penetration, which hit 58% of U.S. sales versus 45% industry average. Key levers included 0% APR financing for 72 months on Bolt models, available to qualified buyers with FICO scores above 680, which drove a 28% uptake in retail purchases and cleared 18 days of U.S. inventory down from 32 days at quarter-end Q1; $7,500 federal IRA lease-cash equivalent bundled with $2,000 state rebates in high-penetration markets like California, where our EV market share climbed to 14.2% from 11.8%; and trade-in guarantees up to $10,000 for ICE vehicles, integrated with our AI-powered valuation tool, boosting conquest sales by 15%—particularly from legacy Detroit players like Ford's F-150 Lightning switchers.

Regionally, North America at 62% of revenue saw incentives average $6,800 per unit, fueling 22% volume growth to 52,000 units. However, with Tesla's recent $2,000 Model Y cut, we responded with elastic pricing on our Bolt, using real-time dynamic algorithms tied to competitor data feeds. This preserved 24.8% regional GM, ahead of Rivian's 19% reported last quarter. Europe at 22% of revenue had promotional intensity lower at $4,200 per unit, emphasizing VAT rebates and our new €5,000 'Green Mobility Bonus' in Germany and France. Volumes grew 8% to 19,000 units, but ASP held at €51,000 thanks to strong demand for the Prime's 520 km WLTP range and V2G capabilities. EU tariffs on Chinese imports up to 38% post-provisional duties shielded us from BYD's Seagull at €25,000, maintaining 11% penetration in the premium segment. China and APAC at 16% of revenue required ultra-competitive pricing, with Bolt ASP at RMB 220,000 or about $31,000 after 12% promotional discounts. We captured 7% market share in the RMB 200k-300k bucket via tie-ins with CATL's Shenxing batteries and free 3-year Supercharger access. Volumes surged 35% to 14,000 units, though margins dipped to 18.2% amid Xiaomi SU7 and NIO ET5 price wars.

Strategically, these moves align with our 'Volume-First, Margin-Second' playbook for 2024, informed by BCG elasticity modeling showing a 1.8x volume response to every $1,000 ASP cut in the mass-market segment. We've layered in technical initiatives like OTA pricing tiers—piloted on 20% of the fleet—allowing post-sale upsells of FSD-equivalent autonomy packs at $8,000, recovering 40% of prior discounts. Inventory optimization via algorithmic lot-matching reduced aged units by 45%, and our supplier scorecard drove 8% YoY COGS deflation on power electronics.

Looking forward, Q3 guidance assumes sustained promotions at $1.6-1.9 billion, targeting 95,000-105,000 units with flat-to-up 1% ASP. We'll taper U.S. incentives if Fed rate cuts materialize, leaning into IRA Section 30D point-of-sale rebates for 2025 MY vehicles. Risks include further Tesla destocking or EU CO2 credit volatility, but our 250,000-unit annualized run-rate positions us for 15% FCF margins by year-end.

As we continue to execute on our mission to accelerate the global transition to sustainable mobility, I'd like to dive deep into our capital expenditure plans and investment priorities for FY2024 and beyond. Our CapEx strategy remains laser-focused on scaling production, driving down costs, and securing technological leadership in the EV space amid a rapidly evolving landscape.

For FY2024, we're guiding for total capital expenditures of $12.5 billion, representing a 25% increase from the $10 billion we deployed in FY2023. This ramp-up reflects our confidence in sustained demand for our flagship models—the Electra Prime sedan and the all-new Apex SUV—coupled with aggressive expansion to capture market share in a segment where global EV sales grew 35% YoY in H1 2024, per recent IHS Markit data. Looking out to FY2025, we anticipate CapEx stabilizing at around $11-13 billion, with a shift toward higher returns as our new facilities reach full utilization.

Breaking this down by our key investment priorities, which align with three pillars: vertical integration for cost leadership, next-gen technology innovation, and geographic diversification to mitigate risks. First, battery production and powertrain vertical integration, which commands 45% of our FY2024 CapEx—or $5.6 billion. Battery costs have fallen 18% YoY to an average of $92 per kWh for our LFP and NMC packs, but we need to go lower to hit our $80/kWh target by 2026. We're investing $3.2 billion in our Nevada Gigafactory Phase 3 expansion, bringing annual cell output to 150 GWh by mid-2025—enough to power over 2 million vehicles. This mirrors Tesla's 4680 scaling playbook but with our proprietary dry electrode process, which cuts manufacturing costs by 15% and energy use by 25%. Additionally, $1.4 billion is earmarked for a new cathode precursor facility in South Carolina, leveraging IRA Section 45X credits that could yield up to $500 million in annual tax incentives. We're prioritizing domestic sourcing of lithium, nickel, and cobalt to de-risk supply chains amid geopolitical tensions—our offtake agreements with Piedmont Lithium and Talon Metals now cover 60% of our needs through 2030.

Second, manufacturing capacity expansion at 30% of CapEx, or $3.75 billion. Vehicle production is our bottleneck, with utilization at our Texas and Berlin plants hovering at 85%. We're allocating $2.1 billion to double output at our upcoming Georgia Gigafactory, on track for first deliveries in Q4 2025, creating 5,000 jobs and qualifying for $1.2 billion in IRA advanced manufacturing credits. In Europe, $1.0 billion goes toward upgrading our Berlin facility to produce our next-gen 800V architecture platforms, countering EU anti-subsidy probes on Chinese imports like BYD's Seagull. This positions us to navigate the EU's 2025 CO2 fleet targets, where non-compliant OEMs face €15 billion in fines. Asia-Pacific gets $650 million for a JV assembly plant in Thailand, targeting ASEAN growth where EV penetration is accelerating to 20% by 2027, per BloombergNEF forecasts.

Third, R&D and autonomy at 15%, or $1.9 billion. Software-defined vehicles are the future—our Electra OS 3.0, with over-the-air updates boosting range by 8% on average, has driven a 22% NPS uplift. We're investing $900 million in L4 autonomy stacks, partnering with Mobileye for radar-LiDAR fusion, aiming for unsupervised robotaxi deployment in select U.S. cities by 2026. Solid-state battery prototypes, targeting 500 Wh/kg density and 1,000+ cycle life, get $500 million; early tests show 30% better cold-weather performance than current Panasonic 2170 cells. This R&D spend is flat YoY as a percentage of revenue but yields 2.5x ROI through IP monetization, including licensing to legacy players like Ford and GM.

Supply chain resilience and charging infrastructure round out the remaining 10%, or $1.25 billion. Vertical integration into rare earths processing—$700 million for a magnet facility in Texas—shields us from China's 90% market dominance. Our Electrify Network expansion adds 5,000 DC fast chargers across North America and Europe, with V4 units delivering 350 kW and Plug & Charge compatibility, addressing the 'range anxiety' barrier where 40% of potential buyers cite infrastructure per J.D. Power surveys.

Strategically, these investments prioritize margin expansion: we expect gross margins to reach 28% by FY2026, up from 22% today, driven by scale economies and a 20% cost-of-goods-sold reduction. Regionally, North America gets 50% of CapEx to capitalize on IRA tailwinds, Europe 25% for tariff-proofing, and APAC 20% to challenge BYD's 30% global BEV share. Risks include raw material volatility—lithium spot prices up 10% in Q2—and permitting delays, but our $8 billion cash runway and $4.5 billion undrawn credit lines provide ample flexibility.

Good afternoon, everyone—I'm thrilled to kick things off with our overall company performance highlights and key achievements. This quarter has been transformative for Electra Motors, underscoring our leadership in the EV transition amid a rapidly evolving global automotive landscape.

First and foremost, we're delivering exceptional top-line growth. Total revenue reached $28.4 billion, a robust 52% year-over-year increase and surpassing our guidance midpoint by 8%. Automotive revenue, our core segment, surged 61% to $24.7 billion, driven by record vehicle deliveries of 512,000 units—up 67% YoY and our highest quarterly volume ever. This marks the ninth consecutive quarter of accelerating delivery growth, outpacing industry leaders like Tesla's Q3 cadence and Rivian's ramp. Energy generation and storage revenue climbed 28% to $2.9 billion, fueled by Megapack deployments exceeding 15 GWh, while services and other revenue grew 35% to $800 million, reflecting higher FSD uptake and SuperHub utilization.

Gross profit expanded to $7.2 billion, yielding a company-wide gross margin of 25.4%—a 720 basis-point improvement YoY and our strongest in two years. Automotive gross margins hit 24.8%, benefiting from scaled production, vertical integration, and favorable mix toward higher-margin models like our Apex SUV and Bolt Pickup. Excluding regulatory credits, which contributed $1.2 billion or about 5% of gross profit, core margins stood at 21.2%, steadily approaching our 25%+ long-term target. Operating income was $4.1 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of $5.8 billion—a 110% YoY jump—demonstrating the power of our cost discipline amid softening raw material prices for lithium and nickel.

On the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with $32.5 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and investments, up $4.2 billion sequentially. Free cash flow generation was stellar at $3.9 billion, or 67% of adjusted EBITDA, enabling $2.5 billion in share repurchases and capex investments totaling $7.8 billion, primarily in our Nevada Gigafactory 3 and new LFP cathode plant in South Carolina. Debt remains low at 0.8x net leverage, giving us ample dry powder for growth.

Turning to key achievements, let's spotlight our production and supply chain mastery. Gigafactory 3 in Nevada achieved full run-rate on our next-gen 4680 structural battery cells, producing 120 GWh annualized capacity—40% ahead of plan. This has slashed per-kWh costs by 28% YoY to under $65, enabling us to price our entry-level Prime sedan at $32,900 with a 320-mile EPA range, undercutting the Chevy Equinox EV while offering superior fast-charging at 250 kW. We've also vertically integrated rare earth processing, securing 85% of our magnet needs domestically via our Texas facility, mitigating China export risks that plagued peers like GM earlier this year.

Regionally, North America remains our fortress, accounting for 58% of deliveries at 297,000 units—up 75% YoY. The Inflation Reduction Act continues to supercharge demand, with $1.8 billion in IRA tax credits flowing through this quarter alone. Our Bolt Pickup captured 12% U.S. pickup market share in Q2, outselling Ford's F-150 Lightning 3-to-1 in the EV segment, thanks to its 450-mile range and 14,000-lb towing capacity. Europe delivered 142,000 units or 28% of total, up 55% YoY despite subsidy cuts in Germany; our Apex SUV now holds 8% BEV SUV share, bolstered by right-hand-drive launches in the UK and partnerships with Volkswagen for co-developed platforms under our MEB-derived Apex Modular Architecture.

In China, we grew 40% to 73,000 units, gaining 2.2 market share points to 4.1% overall BEV share. Facing fierce BYD and CATL competition, we've localized 95% of our Shanghai Gigafactory output using LFP cells, pricing the Prime under RMB 200,000 to tap mass-market demand. APAC ex-China added 18% growth, with strong Thailand and Indonesia ramps via ASEAN free-trade incentives.

Technically, we've pushed boundaries on software and autonomy. Full Self-Driving v12.5 adoption hit 42% of our fleet—double YoY—generating $450 million in high-margin recurring revenue. Our neural net training on 15 billion real-world miles has reduced disengagements by 65% vs. v11, positioning us ahead of Waymo in urban autonomy benchmarks. On the hardware front, the Apex received a mid-cycle OTA update boosting efficiency 12% via aerodynamic tweaks and thermal management, extending range to 380 miles.

Strategically, we're accelerating our 'Electrify Everything' vision. We broke ground on Gigafactory 4 in Mexico, targeting 200 GWh by 2027 with $5 billion IRA funding, creating 12,000 jobs and nearshoring 30% of NA supply chain. Our SuperHub network expanded to 2,800 stalls globally—500 added this quarter—with V4 chargers at 500 kW enabling 200-mile adds in 15 minutes. Sustainability milestones include a 45% YoY drop in Scope 1+2 emissions per vehicle, 92% battery recycling rate via Redwood Materials partnership, and S&P's ESG 'A' rating upgrade.

Market trends affirm our momentum: Global EV sales hit 4.2 million units in Q2 per EV Volumes data, up 32% YoY, with penetration reaching 22%—led by China at 45%. Affordability headwinds are easing with battery prices down 22% YoY to $112/kWh per Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, and policy tailwinds like the EU's 2035 ICE ban and U.S. bipartisan infrastructure persist. While macroeconomic noise like high interest rates tempered fleet sales, consumer demand for our sub-$40k models remains resilient.

Looking ahead, we're raising full-year 2024 guidance: Deliveries to 2.1-2.15 million units up from 2.0-2.1M, revenue to $112-115 billion, and adjusted EBITDA to $22-23 billion. For Q3, expect 550,000-570,000 deliveries and continued margin expansion.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining our Q2 2024 earnings call. I'll walk you through our delivery volumes by model and geographic region. Deliveries remain the north star for our business, directly tying into revenue recognition under ASC 606 and our path to sustained profitability. I'm pleased to report that we achieved total deliveries of 285,000 vehicles in Q2, marking a robust 28% year-over-year increase and a 12% quarter-over-quarter sequential uptick. This exceeded our guidance midpoint of 270,000 units, driven by a favorable model mix shift toward our higher-ASP platforms and ramp-up in key markets despite ongoing macroeconomic headwinds like elevated interest rates and softening consumer demand in certain segments.

By model, our flagship Electra Prime sedan, our volume leader akin to Tesla's Model 3/Y in the mid-premium segment, delivered 142,000 units—up 35% YoY and representing 50% of total mix. This was fueled by our recent OTA software update to V12 autonomy stack, which boosted take rates for our Full Autonomy Package to 42%, adding ~$4,500 ASP uplift per vehicle. Production efficiency at our Texas Gigafactory hit 98% OEE, thanks to our 4680 cell integration, which reduced BOM costs by 15% QoQ.

Next, the Electra Apex Max SUV, our crossover powerhouse competing head-on with the Model Y and Rivian's R1S, clocked 98,000 deliveries—25% YoY growth, or 34% of mix. Demand here was propelled by our new LFP blade battery option, sourced via our JV with CATL, enabling a sub-$45,000 entry price in the US post-IRA incentives. We saw a 22% mix shift to this variant, with gross margins expanding to 28% from 24% last quarter.

Our Electra Titan pickup, launched last year to challenge the Cybertruck and F-150 Lightning, delivered 32,000 units—a stellar 180% YoY ramp from a low base, comprising 11% of mix. Megapack-scale production at our Texas Gigafactory 2 is now at full rate of 10,000/week, supported by structural battery packs that cut weight by 12% and extend range to 520 miles EPA. However, ASP compression to ~$78,000 reflects competitive pricing to capture fleet deals with Hertz and Amazon.

Rounding out the portfolio, our Electra Luxe ultra-premium sedan—positioned against Lucid Air and the Plaid—delivered 13,000 units, flat YoY at 5% mix, as we prioritize margin over volume with 65% FAP attachment rates. Overall model mix shifted +4 points toward higher-margin vehicles, lifting blended ASP to $52,300, up 8% YoY.

Shifting to geographic regions, North America led with 162,000 deliveries—57% of total, +32% YoY. The US accounted for 85% of this at 138,000 units, supercharged by $7,500 IRA point-of-sale rebates, which drove a 45% surge in Prime and Max volumes. Canada added 24,000 amid provincial EV mandates. Supply chain resilience was key here, with domestic 4680 cell content now at 75%, qualifying for full credits and insulating us from Red Sea disruptions.

China delivered 68,000 units—24% of total, +18% YoY but sequentially flat due to fierce competition from BYD's Seagull and Xiaomi's SU7. Our Shanghai Gigafactory hit 95% utilization on Prime exports, but pricing pressure from local OEMs capped ASP at RMB 220,000 or ~$31,000. Positively, our Na-ion battery pilot reduced degradation to <8% after 200,000 km, winning favor with ride-hail fleets like Didi. We're countering with a sub-RMB 150,000 'people's EV' launch in Q1 2025.

Europe contributed 42,000 deliveries—15% of total, +22% YoY, led by Germany 18,000 and Norway 12,000, where Max SUV volumes exploded 55% on 20% VAT rebates and ZEV credits. UK and France added balance amid EU-China tariff hikes to 45% on imports—a tailwind for our Berlin plant ramp, now at 5,000/week. However, softer demand in Italy/Spain reflects subsidy phase-outs; we're addressing with dynamic pricing via our Electra app ecosystem.

Finally, Rest of World—including APAC ex-China, LatAm, and Middle East—delivered 13,000 units, +50% YoY from a small base or 5% mix. Japan/Korea saw initial traction for Titan fleets 4,000 units, while UAE/Saudi pilots for Luxe hit 2,500 amid Vision 2030 diversification.

Key trends and strategic insights: Deliveries outpaced production by 2%, drawing inventory to 18,000 units—healthy ahead of Q3 seasonality. YoY growth beat industry averages global EV deliveries ~15% per Rho Motion, gaining 120 bps share to 4.2% in premium BEV segment. Headwinds include US consumer pull-forward pre-IRA changes and China's overcapacity glut, but tailwinds from our vertical integration—85% in-house powertrain—and software moat FAP recurring rev now $180M quarterly position us strongly.

As we dive into our financial performance, I'd like to spend some time on one of our key profitability metrics: gross margin per vehicle. This is a critical lens for understanding our path to sustainable profitability in the hyper-competitive EV landscape, where scale, vertical integration, and cost discipline separate leaders from laggards.

For Q2, our gross margin per vehicle came in at $13,200, representing a robust 18% year-over-year increase from $11,200 in Q2 2023, and a sequential improvement of $800 or 6% from Q1's $12,400. On a percentage basis, this translates to an overall automotive gross margin of 21.4%, up 320 basis points YoY and 190 bps sequentially. This puts us squarely on track for our full-year guidance of $12,500 to $13,500 per vehicle, with a trajectory toward $15,000+ by end-2025 as our next-gen platforms ramp.

To put this in context, let's break it down by ASP per vehicle and COGS per vehicle. Our Q2 ASP held steady at $52,000, reflecting a healthy mix of our flagship Apex SUV at $58,500 and the more accessible Prime sedan at $45,000. We saw a slight uptick from regulatory credit sales—we recognized $250 million in ZEV and IRA transfer credits, boosting ASP by about $500 per unit. This is comparable to Tesla's playbook, where credits have been a meaningful tailwind, contributing 2-3% to their margins in recent quarters.

On the COGS side, we've driven it down to $38,800 per vehicle, a 12% YoY reduction from $44,000. The biggest lever here has been our aggressive battery cost reductions. Batteries remain 35-40% of total COGS in the EV world, and we've cut our pack costs by 25% YoY through a combination of factors: vertical integration ramp—our Nevada Gigafactory Phase 2 is now producing 40 GWh annually of our proprietary 46XX cylindrical cells similar to Tesla's 4680 but optimized for higher energy density at 280 Wh/kg. This has shaved $2,500 off per pack COGS versus third-party suppliers like LG or CATL, where we'd been paying $120/kWh last year. We're targeting sub-$80/kWh by Q4 2025.

Gigacasting and structural battery packs: We've fully transitioned our Apex line to Giga Press front and rear underbody castings, reducing part count from 400 to 70 and assembly time by 30%. This, paired with our integrated structural battery pack—think BYD Blade tech but with silicon anode additives for 15% more range—has delivered $1,200 in material and labor savings per vehicle. Supply chain resilience: Fixed-price contracts with U.S. steel and aluminum suppliers, locked in post-Ukraine disruptions, combined with IRA localization bonuses, have stabilized raw material costs. Lithium carbonate equivalents are down 40% YoY to $15,000/ton, thanks to our offtake agreements with Piedmont Lithium.

Regionally, in North America, which accounted for 65% of our 28,000 Q2 deliveries, margins hit $14,500 per vehicle—a standout 24% gross margin, fueled by $7,500 average IRA incentives per Apex and minimal tariff exposure. This mirrors Rivian's ramp-up post-VinFast learnings, where U.S.-centric production is a moat. In Europe, at 25% of volume, margins were softer at $11,800 due to VAT rebates tapering and Chinese import pressures from BYD's Seagull at sub-$25,000 landed pricing. EU tariffs on China-sourced cells added 50 bps of headwind, but our Berlin plant's localization—now at 80% EU content—mitigated this, positioning us ahead of legacy OEMs like Volkswagen, who are still posting negative EV margins. China remains our volume engine at 10% of deliveries, with $10,200 margins amid fierce comps from NIO's ET5 and XPeng's P7. Here, our Shanghai JV with CATL is key, enabling sub-$9,000 battery packs and capturing the mass-market LFP segment.

Looking forward, our strategic initiatives are accelerating this trend. Q3 should see another $600 uplift from full Self-Driving software attach rates climbing to 25% at $12,000 ASP, with 90% gross margins—echoing Tesla's software flywheel, which now contributes 10%+ to their per-vehicle profitability; next-gen 'Alpha' platform pilot production: Unboxed manufacturing, direct-drive motors, and 800V architecture targeting $30,000 COGS at scale, versus $38k today; and scale efficiencies: Factory utilization hitting 85% across our U.S. and EU plants, driving fixed cost absorption.

Risks? Ongoing supplier inflation in semis and potential IRA clawbacks if policy shifts post-election. But with $4.2 billion in cash and $2.5B undrawn revolver, we're insulated. Gross margin per vehicle is our North Star, up 18% YoY and trending toward Tesla's 25%+ club. This isn't luck—it's execution on vertical integration, regional tailoring, and tech leadership.

Before I dive into the forward-looking guidance, let me quickly recap our Q2 delivery performance, which sets the stage for what we're outlining today. We delivered 168,000 vehicles globally in Q2, up 22% year-over-year and right in line with our updated guidance range of 165,000 to 175,000 units. This was driven by a strong ramp in our Apex SUV platform, which accounted for 62% of total volume at 104,000 units, benefiting from robust U.S. demand amid IRA-compliant battery sourcing and our refreshed architecture with LFP battery options for improved cost and range efficiency.

Model-by-model, the Prime sedan came in at 38,000 units, flat YoY as we prioritized higher-margin SUV production amid capacity constraints at our Texas Gigafactory 1. Our heavy-duty Titan pickup hit 26,000 units, a 45% YoY increase, fueled by fleet orders from logistics partners like UPS and the ramp of our 4680 structural battery cells, which reduced COGS by 18% per kWh. Regionally, North America represented 58% of volume at 97,000 units, Europe 22% at 37,000, China 15% at 25,000, and the rest of world at 5%. Challenges in China persisted due to intense price competition from BYD's Seagull and Nio's Onvo L60, but our Shanghai JV is gaining traction with localized Apex variants qualifying for NEV credits.

Now, turning to our Q3 delivery volume guidance by model. We're guiding to 190,000 to 210,000 total deliveries for the quarter, implying 13% to 25% sequential growth from Q2 and positioning us for a strong close to FY24. This reflects continued production ramps at Gigafactory Texas, where we're now at 85% utilization on the Apex and Titan lines, and the initiation of 24/7 shifts for our next-gen CTB platform. Apex SUV mid-size crossover, our volume leader: Guiding 120,000 to 135,000 units, or 63% of total Q4 mix. This is up 15% to 30% sequentially, driven by holiday season demand in North America—where IRA Section 30D credits up to $7,500 per vehicle are fully stackable with our base MSRP of $44,990—and Europe, where Euro 7 compliance and our new 400-mile WLTP range variant are resonating. We've seen a 28% YoY increase in FSD take rates to 32%, adding $8,000 to ASP, and inventory drawdown to just 12 days of supply. Strategically, we're allocating 40% of Apex output to enterprise fleets, mirroring Tesla's shift but with our edge in V2G bidirectional charging for commercial apps.

Prime Sedan compact premium: 40,000 to 45,000 units, or 21% of mix. Sequential growth of 5% to 18%, tempered by a deliberate mix shift toward SUVs but boosted by a Q3 price adjustment to $39,990 and software updates enabling unsupervised FSD Beta 12.5. In China, we're targeting 8,000 units via aggressive financing—0% APR for 36 months—to counter Xiaomi's SU7 ramp. Margins here remain strong at 28% gross, thanks to 15% YoY reductions in silicon carbide inverter costs.

Titan Pickup full-size EV truck: 28,000 to 30,000 units, or 15% of mix. Up 8% to 15% sequentially as we exit the initial 4680 cell yield ramp—now at 92% from 75% in Q1—and launch the Mega Range Pack with 520 miles EPA. U.S. dominance here at 90% regional share, with 65% of volumes qualifying for $40,000 commercial clean vehicle credits under IRA 45W. Competition from Ford's F-150 Lightning and Rivian's R1T is noted, but our 800V architecture delivers 350 kW fast charging, giving us a 20% edge in TCO for fleets.

For the full FY24, we're raising our total delivery guidance to 720,000 to 740,000 units, up from 700,000 midpoint previously, implying 28% YoY growth. This incorporates Q3 strength and minimal Shanghai headwinds, with ASP holding at $48,500 despite $2,000 in targeted cuts to stimulate demand elasticity.

Looking to FY25 guidance, which we're introducing today: 1.15 million to 1.25 million total deliveries, a 55% to 70% YoY ramp. Apex SUV: 750k-800k or 65% mix, Gigafactory 3 ramp to 1.2M capacity; Europe expansion via Berlin plant. Prime Sedan: 200k-220k or 18%, affordable trim at $35k; India market entry Q2. Titan: 150k-170k or 14%, 4680 scale to 50 GWh; Cybertruck-like stainless exoskeleton variant. Apex Mini: 50k-60k or 4%, Q3 launch; $25k entry-level vs. BYD Seagull.

Regionally for FY25: North America 60% 690k-750k, Europe 25% 285k-310k with REPowerEU subsidies aiding ramps, China 10% 115k-125k focusing on premium segments, and ROW 5% including Australia and Southeast Asia pilots. Risks include U.S. election policy shifts on IRA, potential EU tariff hikes on Chinese cells mitigated by our 80% North American supply chain, and global lithium carbonate volatility—we've locked 70% of FY25 needs at $12k/ton via long-term offtakes.

Strategically, this guidance underscores our pivot to vertical integration: in-house 4680 production will drive 25% COGS reduction to $105/kWh by year-end, enabling FCF positivity in FY25 at $2.5B midpoint. We're also accelerating Robotaxi unveil in Q1 '25, with 10k-unit pilot production, to unlock high-margin autonomy revenue streams. Supply chain resilience is key—our Texas cathode plant de-risks against CATL dependencies, positioning us ahead of peers like Lucid and Fisker in margin recovery.
